title: Towards Efficient Few-shot Graph Neural Architecture Search via Partitioning Gradient Contribution

problem.claim: Few-shot NAS methods address weight coupling by partitioning supernets, but existing approaches are computationally inefficient and may produce suboptimal partitions.

gap.claim: Existing graph neural architecture search methods are limited to searching either MPNNs or Graph Transformers rather than their combinations.

contributions.claim: The Gradient Contribution method computes cosine similarity among module gradient directions by decomposing the Vector-Jacobian Product during supernet backpropagation.
The partitioning procedure places modules with conflicting gradient directions in separate sub-supernets and groups modules with similar directions together.
The Unified Graph Neural Architecture Search framework searches combinations of Message Passing Neural Networks and Graph Transformers.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly present their analysis of weight coupling through conflicting gradient directions from succeeding-layer modules as a novel perspective.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that Gradient Contribution achieves state-of-the-art supernet partitioning quality and time efficiency.
The authors report that architectures searched by UGAS combined with Gradient Contribution outperform manually designed GNNs and architectures obtained by existing NAS methods.
The authors report that ablation studies support the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

narrative_sequence.summary: Few-shot NAS methods partition supernets to address weight coupling, but existing approaches have efficiency and partition-quality limitations.
The paper attributes weight coupling primarily to conflicting gradient directions imposed by modules in succeeding layers.
Gradient Contribution measures gradient-direction similarity and uses it to construct sub-supernets, while UGAS searches combinations of MPNNs and Graph Transformers.
The authors report improvements in partitioning quality, time efficiency, searched-architecture performance, and ablation effectiveness.

source_observation.claim: Partitioning decisions are based on similarity or conflict among module gradient directions.

interpretation.claim: Gradient interactions can serve as a practical signal for reducing interference when sharing weights across architecture choices.

application.claim: For other shared-supernet search problems, measure training-signal interactions before grouping components into shared parameter spaces.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that gradient-direction similarity is sufficient across tasks, architectures, or training regimes.

unknowns: Datasets, experimental settings, and evaluation metrics are not specified.
The compared NAS methods and manually designed architectures are not identified.
Quantitative performance and efficiency results are not provided.
The scope and computational cost of the ablation studies are not described.
